speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALE OR TRANSFER OF SHARES OF STOCK
speechtext:
May I remind the house and the country that in the budget speech delivered on March 1, notice was given of a proposed change in part seven of the Special War Revenue Act, concerning the sale or transfer of shares of stock. It was provided that this change should go into effect on the 1st of May, next Wednesday. It is now apparent that the necessary amending bill may not be ready to receive royal assent before that date and it is proposed that the revised rates shall not be effectual until July 1. The officers of the National Revenue department have been notified accordingly.
The abolition of the Special War Revenue Act tax on cables, telegrams, railway and other tickets becomes effective on May 1.

On the orders of the day:

I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, or the Solicitor General, or whichever power or authority the question should be directed to, in respect of a petition which was presented to the house yesterday by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre), a petition which asked for the suppression of a paper called "Vapaus." I should like to ask whether the officers of the house have examined that petition, and whether they have formally accepted or rejected it. In connection with the question, if I am in order,
I should like to point out that Bourinot, third edition, page 348, says:
AH petitions should be respectfully and temperately worded. The house will refuse to receive them if they contain any reflections on the king or his representative in Canada, or on the action of parliament, or on any of its committees, or on the courts of justice, or affect "the legal and social positions of individuals."
I believe that petition shows disrespect to His Majesty inasmuch as it asks for_ the suppression of liberty, whereas His Majesty stands for liberty to all British people. In the next place it infringes the law.

The hon. gentleman, to be in order, should give notice and move that the petition be not received in spite of the report which has been made. The matter is not debatable just now, but if the hon. gentleman will give notice and move that the petition be not received for the reason he alleges, he will be in order.
Has the petition been examined?
All petitions are examined by the officers of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: After they have been presented?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So the petition is in the hands of the law officers of the house?

Certainly. It is not before the house now. I will see what report has been made and will inform the house at

I desire to ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) a question, of which I have not given him notice, but I think he will be able to answer it without notice. I have received a telegram regarding the awarding of the air mail contracts for western Canada. It reads:
Understand Western Canada Airways of Winnipeg will be granted entire western air mail contracts. When in Ottawa last month postal minister assured me that our company would be given consideration. You are aware I formed Great Western Airways and pioneered aviation here with board of directors fuliy able to finance air mail service between Winnipeg and Calgary. No contract has been awarded for that service yet. That company is being communicated with for an offer.
Thank you.

speechtext: I did not understand that we had passed the item with regard to a public building in Calgary. I would like the minister to give some explanation of this item of 8300,000 for a public building in Calgary.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend was present last night when the matter was under discussion. This amount is required towards the erection of a new public building to house all the government offices at Calgary. The proposed building will be an eight storey stone and brick structure situated on Eighth avenue at the corner of First Street east. The building will have a frontage of 158 feet 9 inches on Eighth avenue by a depth of 120 feet on First street east. The new building proposed to be erected at Calgary was advertised in March, 1920, and tenders were received amounting to approximately $1,400,000. Those were the tenders at that time, and that is the 'best estimate that I can give to my hon. friend of what the probable cost will be. The building will contain 2,808,307 cubic feet which, at the price of $1,400,000, will be between 52 and 53 cents per cubic foot.

There is nothing in the votes and proceedings or in Hansard to show that Vote 127 was passed last night.

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
Hansard will show that this particular item was agreed to last night.

It should appear in
Hansard.
It is in Hansard. My hon. friend will see that the item was agreed to last night.

May I suggest the desirability of having that building faced with granite? When this building was discussed in 1914, it will be recalled that there was an item in the estimates of $250,060, but then the war came on. In 1920 tenders were called for a building of stone and brick. There is a very fine quarry of granite in the constituency of the Minister of National Health, and that granite has been found very serviceable. It makes an excellent building material. I was hoping that possibly alternative tenders might be called for the utilization of that granite. The Minister of National Health knows the granite to which I refer.
It is only fair to my hon. friend to say that the present recommendations do not provide for granite proper. As my hon. friend knows, it is much more expensive.

It might not be very
much more expensive.

However, I shall be very
glad to consider the proposal of having alternative tenders, but I do not think we can make an exception of the city of Calgary in that respect.

When must the tenders
be in?

My hon. friend' will understand that we will begin to prepare the plans now. We have the old plans that were provided in 1920. Tenders were called for then. Of course my hon. friends will readily understand that we are doing nothing by way of preparing new plans or anything else until the estimate is passed in the house.

Of course, the plan could
be prepared and tenders called for on the supposition that the item is going through. I say that in justification of my question. The calling for tenders does not necessarily mean the job is going through anyway.

No, but perhaps my hon. friend knows the difficulties in the architect's branch, and this applies practically throughout Canada. Owing to the fact that during the war years there was no public building going on
here, we are not as flush of architects and draughtsmen as we would have been if our building program had been so extensive as to provide work for them. A great many of our architects at that time went across to the United States. Our requirement is that they must have resided here for three years to qualify for a position. The present staff is fully occupied on buildings with regard to which the estimates have been passed and there is no question of their going on.

I assume that the usual
fair wage clause will be inserted in the contract and that as much as possible local labour will be employed1?

We will advertise for
tenders. There will be no doubt about the fair wage clause, but I do not think -it would be fair to the contractor to say that he must take labour from any particular district. He will have to be his own judge to a considerable extent as to that. Naturally labour will come from the district pretty largely.

I think that as far as
possible the tradesmen and labourers should be local people, and that outsiders should not be brought in to lower the wages.

I wish to express my appreciation to the government for having listened to those eloquent appeals which I made some years ago for this post office, and for having decided ultimately to take action. I see now the proper way to go about these things, and I shall know better in the future how to proceed.
In spite of what my hon. friend says, this building is going to be put up shortly.

The hon. member for
Wetaskiwin says he knows how to proceed to get these things. I think for the benefit of the house he might tell us a little more as to the proper procedure. I should like to know.

Item agreed to.
Vegreville-public building, $35,000.
The minister might explain this item.

Vegreville is 75 miles east of Edmonton. This amount of $35,000 is required for the erection of a public building on the comer of Main street and Second avenue in the town of Vegreville for postal and customs purposes. The proposed building will be a one and a half storey brick structure, 45 feet long by 34 feet wide, with a one storey annex 11 feet by 18. It will provide accommodation for the postal service and living quarters for the caretaker. Requests for the building have been received, at various times, from Mr. White, M.P. in 1910, the Hon. Mr. Calder in 1919, the Vegreville board of trade in 1919, the Vegreville Liberal Association in 1924, the Vegreville board of trade, transmitted by Mr. W. T. Lucas, M.P. in 1924. Requests have also come from other sources.
How large is the place?

The population is 1,852,
according to Heaton's Annual. The postal revenue for 1927-28 amounted to $11,529.36 and the customs revenue for the same period, 811,116.91. The department have asked for the facilities.

This will be used as a
customs building also.
Yes.

The town of Vegreville is a very beautiful place and I am glad to see the item in the estimates this year. The post office building at the present time is a miserable affair, and in view of the importance of this town and the significance of such a building to the community I am pleased that the minister has submitted this
item. The hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Blatchford) knows the town very well; he makes an annual airplane trip there. I am sure the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) also knows a little about about the place. He knows it is an excellent town and needs this accommodation very badly.

The vote of $50,000 for the Trail building, is one item to which the government has given its serious consideration. The minister has certainly carried out his intention of providing additional postal and customs facilities in a community where he knows the accommodation has not been adequate although the need has been urgent. Trail is the greatest metallurgical centre in the British Empire, as hon. members know, and last year we were honoured with a visit from the Governor General, who officiated at the laying of the cornerstone of perhaps the handsomest city hall in the interior of British Columbia. I only hope that the Minister of Public Works will similarly honour us during the coming summer. Item agreed to.
Experimental farms-replacements, repairs, improvements, etc., $100,000.
I should like to ask the minister where the Dominion experimental farms in Canada are located.

The farms are at Charlottetown,, Summerside, Kentville, Nappan, Fredericton, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Cap Rouge, St. Joachim, Lennoxville, Farnham, L'Assomption, La Ferme, Kapuskasing, Harrow, Morden, Brandon, Indian Head, Rosthern, Scott, Swift Current, Lethbridge, Lacombe, Windermere, Summerland, Agassiz, and Sidney.

The reason I ask is this: I notice there are a number of these farms in the maritime provinces and in Quebec while in Ontario the farm furthest west is at Kapuskasing. The other day I received a resolution from a farmers' organization in my constituency or at least in that section of the country recommending that the government establish an experimental farm on the north shore of lake Superior.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends laugh at that; they laugh at anything which does not affect their own constituencies, but perhaps it is not so easy to laugh when we are dealing with a government that is not very anxious to do anything in our constituencies.
Does my hon. friend think that is a fair statement for him to make, representing the constituency of Fort William?

I think that is a fair statement. My hon. friend is rather touchy; he thinks I should be content because there is a little dredging being done in the harbours of Port Arthur and Fort William this year. As a matter of fact the money being spent there is being expended for the national welfare of this country, to facilitate the handling of the wheat of my hon. friends from the west. I am not unresponsive to that; I am glad it is being done for the good of the whole country, and naturally one does not object to money being spent in his riding, but as a matter of fact this is a national undertaking.

Supply-Public Works-Experimental Farms
My hon. friend referred to the expenditure of money in the ridings of hon. gentlemen on this side of the house.

My hon. friends opposite had a hearty laugh when I mentioned the need for an experimental farm in that thousand miles of territory extending from Kapuskasing on the east to Winnipeg. According to the list read by the minister there are experimental farms every two or three hundred miles or less in the eastern provinces, but here is a long stretch of country without one. The supporters of the minister laughed at my request, and I think I have a right to take exception to that. When I look at these estimates I find that a large proportion of hon. gentlemen opposite are looked after much more carefully than are the members on this side of the house.
They do not say so.

The estimates say so.
However, I wish to point out the need of my section of the country as put forward by the farmers who have gone into a bush country, as compared with the farmers who have gone to the prairies where farming is much easier. The last experimental farm in Ontario is at Kapuskasing; I do not know where the first experimental farm is in Manitoba, but I believe it is in the neighbourhood of Winnipeg.
It is at Morden.

That is southwest of Winnipeg, and that leaves an area of perhaps 800 miles without an experimental farm. That is a section of the country where it is very difficult for men to cut out their homes, because it is bush country. We all know they have to meet greater problems than the farmers on the prairies; their problems are those which were met years ago by the farmers in eastern Ontario, in Quebec and in the maritime provinces.

And in the
prairie provinces also.

No, they are not in the same class at all; the men who go into these bush lands in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, the maritime provinces or in British Columbia have a much more difficult time than the men who go to the prairies, where the lands are cleared to a large extent by nature.

They are not
cleared in the northern parts.

I differ with my hon.
friend.

I think you are right
there.

there so he does not know.

sections.

Public Works which pays for the repairs.

the attention of the hon. member to a fact

settled.

But when the Department of Agriculture does approach the minister, as I am endeavouring to have them do, I do ask him to give every consideration to this matter. The territory 1 have mentioned is rather a long overnight's walk from Kapuskasing, and it is a territory where it is very difficult for pioneers to go in and farm at the present time. The minister has been there and he knows it very well.
I know it quite well.

When this matter comes before the minister I am sure that he will give it fair consideration. The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) is sitting right beside him at the present moment and he usually supports me in any request for northern Ontario. I know if the minister will ask the opinion of the hon. member to his right he will back me up in what I am asking for that section of the country.
I will tell the hon. member that the hon. member for Nipissing always supports any sugestions which are made for that part of Ontario.
We always stand together; I help him out too.
He has been perhaps even more successful than my hon. friend from Fort William, but I think he is rather surprised to hear that he is still a bit dissatisfied.
The minister nearly made a slip then.

The decision as to where an experimental farm is to be located is a matter for the consideration of the Department of Agriculture and I would suggest to my hon. friend that his remarks would have had more weight if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr Motherwell) had been present in the house.
I will do it over again when he is present.
I will be very glad to pass it on to the minister.

I am afraid that is a lefthanded compliment which the minister has paid me, and I think he paid me another left-handed compliment when he pointed out to the house that the member for Nipissing is always more successful than I am.
I would like to ask the minister if these are really experimental farms. The minister read a long list to the house and if they are all experimental farms, it is something new to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are learning something every day.
I have not an intimate knowledge of all of them, but a list of experimental farms and branch farms was given to me.
If the minister will look into that matter I think he will find that a large number of them are nothing more than demonstration farms. We have not that number of real experimental farms in Canada.
Probably so.
I know the one at La-combe is called a demonstration farm.
Did the list which the hon. minister read include demonstration and experimental farms?
It included what are called branch farms.

Flags for Dominion public buildings, $5,000.

In my movements about the country I have observed flags flying at night, and the result is that the flags are destroyed. With respect to flying flags there are instructions that should have been in force in this country for a very long time. I have noticed, for instance, the flag on the post office building here is frequently put up until it falls to pieces and another one is put in its place.
What post office does my hon. friend refer to?

I have observed this
one at times. The situation has been remedied recently.
Does my hon. friend mean in Ottawa?
Yes.
Does my hon. friend say that he has seen the flag flying after sundown?

I have certainly seen it
flying after sundown.
I think he is forgetting.

What is more, I have noticed the same thing many times in other places in the country. Hon. members will remember passing through communities and seeing flags flapping to pieces against the poles. Last year we spent $5,000 in buying new flags and this year we are going to spend another $5,000. Why should we wear out flags by leaving them up at night? Purchase of stamp cancelling machines, $55,000.

Mr. Chairman, I think
we should have some explanation of this item. The stamp cancelling machines used in Canada have in some instances been leased; in others, purchased. I dare say the hon. minister has received, as I have, a communication from a firm in the United States that was prepared to manufacture in this country and sell to postmasters stamp cancelling machines. They were not permitted to do so because the postal department would not permit the postmasters to use them. That, of course, is a matter for the Post Office Department, not the Department of Public Works. What stamp cancelling machines are being purchased for $55,000, where are they being used, and by whom are they being manufactured?

This amount is required
to complete the payment on twenty-five stamp cancelling machines purchased by authority of an order in council passed on June 8, 1927, from Mr. G. H. Robert of Montreal at a cost of $2,500 for each machine. Delivery of three machines was made in 1928-29 and the sum of $1,500 was paid on account of the purchase price of same pending a final acceptance by the Post Office Department. The remaining twenty-four machines will not be delivered until 1929-30, and consequently it is necessary to revote the sum of $55,000 for payment of them.
Where are they made?
I think they are manufactured in Montreal by the Robert concern. The information I have is that they are machines of the A type, manufactured by G. H. Robert of Montreal.

There has been a good
deal of discussion about these machines. Have they proved satisfactory? I received a communication stating that only a few of them had been delivered, and that they had not

Supply-Public Works-Miscellaneous
been entirely satisfactory, also that offers had been made from other sources but the department had said no. If these machines were required when the order was given for twenty-five, why is it that two years are allowed to elapse with only three delivered, and the other twenty-two net to be delivered until some time next year? It was also alleged that these machines were oovered by an American patent and were assembled in Canada, not manufactured in the sense in which that term is properly used.

I think there is something in what my hon. friend says as to these machines being largely in an experimental stage. The latest report I have from the Post Office Department is that for years the practice has been to rent stamp cancelling machines manufactured by the Postage Meter Company of Stamford, Connecticut. At present ninety-two machines are rented at an annual rental of $15,850. This company offered to sell these machines outright to the Post Office Department for the sum of $63,050, but the report on them was not altogether favourable. It was thought that it would be better to purchase these machines. I fancy the reason for the revote is that the department is trying the machines out t-o make absolutely sure that they are satisfactory before the balance of the purchase price is paid. The desire of the department is to buy a Canadian machine if it will fill the requirement, that is, a machine made in Canada, rather than continue the practice that has been followed in the past.

There is a contract or
there is not. If there is a contract, we should see it. My information is that the machine parts are brought into the country and duty paid upon them and then they are assembled here. That may be inaccurate, but I do know that a firm in New York offered to establish in Canada a factory to produce stamp cancelling machines, which they said they could sell for about $250 apiece. They offered to sell them to postmasters throughout the country, the larger machines to be operated by power and the smaller by hand, but the Post Office Department declined the offer. It seems to me that we should have definite information as to whether or not these machines are being manufactured or assembled in Canada, and whether or not they are covered by an American patent. If the latter is the fact, then of course we are no further ahead than when buying an American machine.

The Postmaster General
would be able to answer the question. We have only a limited amount of detail but

I have not the agreement here, but there was a stipulation that a quantity of parts should be kept in store in case replacements were needed, the services of a mechanic to be at the disposal of the department for one year free of charge. The proposal of the Postage Meter Company is not favourable for the following reasons: Their products are not manufactured in this country.
The duty, freight, sales tax, etc., are not taken into consideration.
The speed of the Canadian machine is double the American type, and the date and time changes are automatic, eliminating the present handling of loose type and consequent delays in the despatch of mail; further, the centrifugal system of inking insures a gradual flow and precludes the damaging of letters as is
common at the present time	
Will you, therefore, kindly proceed to supply this department with the Canadian machine.

The machines were bought

That is about the size of
it. We were asked to secure the revote inasmuch as the machines were still-

-being tried out.

two years to test machines like these. As a layman I should think that a month would do it. It is purely a matter of seeing that they stamp at the rate per minute called for

Why is the Department of Public Works concerned with this matter at all? This is a question of supplies for the Post Office Department; why does not that department look after it? Why charge this $55,000 to public works?

This is the type of office equipment which apparently has always been included in supplies furnished by the Department of Public Works to the Post Office Department. It is included among such supplies as lock boxes and office furniture.

No; but the mail bag is hardly office equipment in the same sense as a cancelling machine. The Department of Public Works, possibly, might very well have contended that the Post Office Department should supply these machines, but apparently equipment of this character has always been included as part of office furniture supplied by this department in connection with its buildings. I suppose that is the connection.

conveyers, tractors, pick-up tables and so forth which we supply. I think it may be said generally that the list includes all mechanical equipment that goes into buildings we construct.

I mean, including all
machines and other equipment such as pickup tables, conveyers and so forth.
I cannot give that information.
Were any tenders called for in connection with the contract?
I should not imagine it was a contract that could be let by tender, because there is only one manufacturer in Canada.

There is a real complaint to be made in this regard. The Raymond Corporation offered to construct a factory in Canada to supply, not these identical machines but stamp obliterating machines, and the government declined to permit the sale of them to postmasters; at any rate, it declined to permit postmasters to buy them if they wanted to pay for them themselves, in face of the contract which had been made with the Robert Manufacturing Company.
I understand, of course, that the Minister of Public Works in a sense is not responsible for that contract, which was made by the department under the control of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). But we should see the contract itself in order to arrive at some conclusion as to why an exclusive right like this should be given to a company-for it amounts to that when you decline to permit anyone else to sell similar machines to postmasters. You refuse to allow others who desire to establish a factory in Canada to sell large and small machines for use by country postmasters, and other equipment as well, such as power machines, hand machines and so forth. In the meantime these experiments are going forward and only three machines have been installed', according to the minister; I thought there were five. One of these machines, I am advised, is in the Ottawa post office. Is that correct?

I do not know. The fact that we have not been requested to pay the money but to revote it is perhaps the reason why we have not scrutinized the present status

of the matter as carefully as we should have done if we were asked to pass an order in council providing the money. Only $1,500 has been paid out of the whole vote-

Mr. BOY'S:	Is there anything in the contract giving this company the exclusive right to supply these machines and preventing others in Canada from supplying similar equipment?
I think the contract is exclusive; if any hon. gentleman wants to see the contract, so far as I am concerned all the papers in my department in this connection are available.

At the moment I would not
think my leader altogether irilght ion this point; I would think the contract should have been made by the Public Works department at the request of the Post Office Department.
I think we make all contracts where we have to pay the money.

Then the minister might produce the contract, because the exclusive feature strikes me as rather serious. If the contract is to be in force for five or six years it means that the whole thing is in the hands of this one concern.

My hon. friend will understand that this is a very different class from an article for which there is a very general demand all over the country. This is something which never has been manufactured in Canada, something we were unable to obtain here previously. If an industry can be built up in Canada the government are anxious that that be done.
I am glad the minister is coming to that point of view; we have 'been advocating that policy for a long time.

We are agreed upon something, anyway. I think my hon. friend will see the fairness of saying to these people, " Go ahead and try to work it out and if you can get a machine equally satisfactory or almost as satisfactory as this machine you will get the business." In the meantime I think they should have a free hand and should be protected from outsiders, otherwise they would not enter into the contract.

Without knowing what is in the contract and without the minister being able to inform us it would be improper and undesirable to offer any criticism, but it does
seem to me that this is a matter which might well engage the attention of the committee. Perhaps before disposing of this item we should see the contract, so I think the minister might let the item stand until the contract is produced.
I would direct my hon.. friend's attention to the fact that this is a re-vote; the same item has been passed several times.
That is one of the reasons for this criticism. If everything were satisfactory a re-vote would not be necessary; the money would have been paid long ago.
I would rather pass the item now if possible, and I will undertake to supply my hon. friend with all the information.

So far as I am personally concerned of course I take the word of the minister at once, but is it really vital that this item should be passed at this time? If all the estimates of the minister were going through I would not try to hold them up because of this, but I do not suppose they are all going through now. However, I will leave it to the judgment of the minister; it seems to me that the request is fair and might be complied with, but if the minister prefers to pass the item and produce the contract later that will be quite all right. When will the contract be produced?
I will produce it at the next sitting, before my estimates are completed.
Then this item might be passed on the understanding that we can refer back to it if we wish to do so after the production of the contract.
Very well.

from the taps is supplied by the city. There is a certain amount of bottled water supplied in the House of Commons and in several of the other departmental buildings but that is not provided under this contract.

bottled water come from?

tests the city water.

I cannot tell you anything about that; we do not buy it and we do not pay for it. It is paid for through the estimates of the House of Commons.

Can the minister tell us
whether or not it is safe to drink the tap water at present? I am asking that question very seriously.

The city officials say it
is safe, and I drink it every day.

I am given to
understand that the city water is not absolutely safe. What about this Tally Ho water? We should have some information; if that is perfectly safe water we should know by whom the examination is made.

I want to give all the information I can but that water is paid for out of the estimates of the House of Commons. My good friend the Sergeant-at-Arms tells me that the Tally Ho Company supplies certificates once a month showing the tests of the water which have been made, but the payment for the Tally Ho water is not made under the Public Works estimates.

I think the question
raised by the hon. member for Kingston is very important. This subject has been under consideration year after year and apparently no negotiations have been entered into with the city of Ottawa leading to an adequate supply of pure water. The very fact that 
the water must be chlorinated is sufficient evidence that we are taking a certain amount of risk when we drink it, and I think I am within the bounds of truth when I say there is great danger of this water being contaminated by sewage. Its very appearance suggests that; one almost dislikes to take a bath in it, let alone drink it. I have not drunk city water since I came to Ottawa; I have been afraid to do so, and when the government pays $45,000 a year for water presumably for this and other government buildings I think that should warrant us entering into negotiations with the city. I would ask the minister if anything has been done in that connection.

No, I think not. The
government has contracted for the best water supply available, and this is the water which is used by the citizens of Ottawa. According to reports which have emanated from the city council I understand that a filtration plant is about to be established, but we must remember that the water supply for this city has been a difficult problem. However, it is a municipal problem and this seems to be the best arrangement we are able to make at present.

I am not criticizing the minister for his arrangement because all municipal governments have to have some pressure put upon them. It is a well known fact that the city of New Orleans, which takes its water from the Mississippi river, has one of the purest supplies of drinking water on the continent, while the city of Ottawa with probably 110,000 people is pumping its water out of the Ottawa river which carries the sewage from the northern country. They have nothing more than a chlorinating system and it is quite patent to anyone that if that system should be defective for twenty-four hours there is the possibility of a typhoid epidemic. The department is probably one of the largest contributors in the form of revenue and some pressure should be brought to bear upon the municipal government to have them supply pure drinking water to the people.

In fairness to the oity
authorities, I think it should be mentioned that there has been a commission investigating the problem and I think they have decided upon a filtration plant. What the member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) says is absolutely correct, but we should not forget that the city is considering this problem at the present time and has under consideration the construction of a filtration plant to properly filter the water.

Supply-Public Works-Ottawa
What is being done now?
It is being chlorinated.

I do not think the minister should be satisfied with the statement that this water is pathologically examined every day. I am rather surprised that a statement is submitted only once a month for the Tally-Ho water. That is not sufficient and does not give protection to the public. One or two oases of typhoid in the city of Ottawa might very well start an epidemic over the whole Dominion, when we consider that these are the days of quick transportation by automobile and train. I think there should be some statement from the minister that the water has been examined every day, and there should be a certificate of safety. There is no question that chlorination is quite safe, but the mere statement as to chlorination is not satisfactory unless it is regularly done. The minister should be able to furnish some statement of a safe water supply every day, or there should be a statement given on the days when it is not considered safe. The city can look after itself but there should be a statement issued in the house on the days when the water is found to be wrong. When we come to these estimates we can look into the matter of the Tally-Ho water and see that a statement is given more often than once a month.

I understood the minister to say that these elevators would thereafter 'be operated on that day. The minister's statement was:
However, if it is found that anybody is suffering inconvenience on account of inadequate elevator facilities, either going up or going down, we will endeavour to rectify it.
I would point out to the minister that this condition is not rectified as yet. His deputy minister is beside him and I understand he is the man in charge of the elevators and I expect him to carry out the distinct understanding which I had with the minister on that occasion. I trust that I will not have to bring this matter up again and that these elevators will be operated for the balance of the session.

Perhaps the minister will remember that we discussed last year the possibility of using the electric current from the turbines at New Edinburgh. One hundred thousand dollars represents interest at 5 per cent on $2,000,000, and I would like to know from the minister what progress has been made in connection with the utilization of these turbines.

The information is that
the requirements for research purposes will take up practically all the power that we have at that site. It is the intention to utilize the power at the Edinburgh mills for supplying all power in connection with the research work, and the information is that there will be no surplus.

The difference between

I would like to refer
back to the question of elevators, and to ask the minister what salaries the elevator attendants receive. I understand that most of the men are returned soldiers and that their salary is only about S80 per month. If that is so I would ask that that salary should be raised to at least $100 per month.
Supply-Public Works-Ottawa
My hon. friend is correct in regard to their being returned men. There are twenty-six operators at $105 a month, twenty-three at $100, two at $95 and fifteen at $90.
Why the discrimination if they are all doing the same class of work? Why should there not be a minimum salary of $100 a month?
We start them at a minimum and they rise to a maximum.
They can go up to $105? Mr. ELLIOTT: Yes.
And those who have recently entered the service are at $90?
Yes.
Are they mostly married men?
We do not have information as to that.
They ought to receive a salary of at least $100 a month, and I should like the minister to consider the matter.

They will after they are in the service a certain length of time. My hon. friend, I think, will agree with me that a new man who has just been hired, should not receive as much as a man who has been in the service for some time.
It does not take long to learn how to run an elevator. After a month's work I think, if they are returned men, they ought to get $100 a month.

They are off.

They are employed all the time.
What are they doing?

They are running elevators.
Mr. ADSHEM): Is the salary paid once or twice a month?
Once a month.
I think it ought to be paid at least twice a month to workingmen.
My deputy informs me that it was paid once a month prior to the last payment, but they are now being paid twice a month.

Does the minister not think the government might find some work for these men who are off at the end of the session? Could something not be found for them somewhere to give them an all-year-round job?

I am sure that different
departments, if they have anything on which they can use them, will try to use them, but I would point out that if you are to keep-expenditures within reasonable bounds, you can pay the men only for the time they are actually employed; you cannot undertake to-fumish employment for the balance of the year for what are called temporary employees. Many of them fit into other positions during the rest of the year, but there is no assurance of that.

I quite agree on general principles with the minister, but in my opinion the working man or woman is the last person on whom to start economizing. After all, what would $90 a month for five months for ten or fifteen people amount to?' These people have to live, and if we expect to have them here in the winter time as trained men, the government should endeavour to find some work for them in order to-give them continuity of employment.

I think that is a fair

I might say that the

The number of buildings,

accounted for 880 of the 900. Where are the other 20?

I understand the charwomen working in the House of Commons are allowed' sick leave pay up to four days on presentation of a doctor's certificate, but that the charwomen in the outside service, who are doing work which is more regular and of a permanent nature, are not allowed this privilege. It seems unreasonable that they should not be given the same consideration as the smaller number of women working in the House of Commons.
I think the same applies to both.
But it does not.
I am afraid I did not understand my hon. friend as clearly as I should. Is he referring to whole-time employees or to charwomen?

I am referring to charwomen in both cases. I understand that the charwomen employed in the House of Commons are allowed sick leave up to four days on production of a doctor's certificate. Will the same consideration be given to charwomen in the outside buildings?

The charwomen who are getting sick leave are under another jurisdiction. I am not going to criticize its action one way or another in this respect; but I do not think my hon. friend will say that we should establish the practice of granting sick leave to employees who are working only two and a half hours a day.
Who makes the regulation as to sick leave with regard to the charwomen employed here
The Speaker.
That seems very extraordinary to me.
Are these people under the Civil Service Commission?
No.
They are appointed by whom?
Those in the char service are appointed' by my department; those engaged here are appointed by the Speaker.
Who determines their remuneration?
The Department of Public Works.
Do you not think you are paying them an extremely low rate? What is your opinion?

Had my hon. friend been listening he would have found my opinion to be that they are pretty well paid. What does he pay to a woman who comes to work at his house for two hours and a half a day?
I think $1.25 is very good pay.
I just wanted to know your opinion.
I expressed it before.

The general opinion throughout the country is that the smaller employees of the government, those who have no professional training, are paid at much too low a rate. I think it is not consistent with the dignity of the government to pay such low wages simply because they can get away with it.
I know this is a matter in which my hon. friend is interested, and I am sure he wants to be fair about it.
That is why I spoke.
The very fact that the crowd of applicants is as great as it is is the best evidence that they can do better here than in any other place in Ottawa.

I think that is simply evidence that there are a lot of unfortunate women in very poor circumstances. The amount is not extravagant; in fact I do not think it is enough.
Has the minister forgotten about that prosperity statement?

I think he would do well to copy the example of the Speaker in allowing them sick leave for a certain number of days if they submit a doctor's certificate. Although they work only two and a half hours a day, the minister overlooks the fact that they often have to come a long distance, which means two journeys a day. These people should be given a little consideration in time of sickness.

Why should private
secretaries or even deputy ministers have telephones given them? Has that been always the custom? Is that one of the perquisites of office?

Perhaps my hon. friend
will recall the discussion in this regard a year ago. For years this has been the system. At one time it was thought that it should be abolished so far as private secretaries were concerned; that was twelve years ago. Some of the private secretaries felt that inasmuch as these telephones were being used largely in communication back and -forth in departmental business, and with the salaries they were receiving, they did not need telephones unless they were supplied. The telephones were consequently taken out and I believe the new order of things lasted about a week, after which they reverted to the present system. That was during the Meighen administration.

No, but they just were
not so easily communicated with as before, and it was not advantageous to government business. I do not believe that if my hon. friend were running the office he would do with fewer telephones.

I run a business and I

Are long distance tolls

If on government business.
Surely this is "a vicious principle," to quote the Prime Minister; it is worse than a vicious principle.

"A thoroughly vicious
principle."

Here are ministers receiving salaries of $10,000 and deputy ministers receiving the same, and the minister comes to parliament and seriously asks this house and the country to believe that the public business would be held up if these people were not supplied with this perquisite. The thing is ridiculous. If ministers need more money, if -the deputies need more money, it is the duty of the government to come to parliament and say so and have the thing done openly. I think the one thing that is disgusting the public to-day with all people in public life-and we all have to contend with it-is the fact that these things are not done openly. We come here, and the general opinion in the country is that we are getting all kinds of perquisites, which I grant we are not, that are worth a great deal of money to us; in fact, we are looked upon more or less as a species of grafter. It is just things of



Supply-Public Works-Ottawa
this sort, not done openly, that create in the country at large that misconception of our work and duties here. If these people need more money the government should come out boldly and give it to them, but not take the money out of the public treasury for things which after all are not in the public interest. Where is the minister or deputy minister today who would not have a telephone in his house, and where is there a telephone in anyone's house which is not used largely for domestic purposes? Once or twice, or three times in a week there may be a business call, but after all the telephone is largely for the convenience of the family and not at all in the public interest. I for one object to this sort of expenditure.

Will the minister tell us exactly what perquisites the members of the government get outside their salaries. What advantages do they receive? I might explain, as the previous speaker said, that a good many people talk about the perquisites of the ministers; for instance, I understand that they are all supplied with automobiles and chauffeurs at the public expense. Apparently they are supplied with telephones also, and I would like to know what other perquisites there are.

I do not know that I can think of any others at the moment; I think my hon. friend has covered them pretty well. He has a number of colleagues who are perhaps able to tell him just as well as any member of the government could. His question is quite proper and I do not object to it; there is the car, the chauffeur and the telephone.
Gasoline.

You cannot run a car
without gasoline. As far as I am concerned, if there is anything the ministers are not given which my hon. friend could suggest and which would assist the ministers in carrying out their duties, I will be in favour of it. I will support anything which will increase the efficiency or conserve the time of the ministers, because I think that is necessary.
I do not want to be understood as saying it is wrong, but I want to point out that a minister would be just as efficient if he paid for his own car and chauffeur.

That would apply to
telephones also.

That is quite true, but
probably he would not use them quite so much.

Supposing I wish to
call up the minister on the telephone tonight and his phone is busy owing to its use by the members of his family in connection with social engagements. Would that be increasing the efficiency of the minister? Are these telephones marked " for business only " or are they available for the social requirements of the entire family?

As far as my own telephone is concerned it is used for all the social engagements of all the members of the family. If my hon. friend or any of his colleagues wishes to call me up in a social way, so far as I am concerned that telephone will be always at his disposal. I should not think he would want any government to be carried on by ministers who would not allow their telephones to be used for social purposes. So far as I am concerned I shall be very glad to have him use my telephone any time he wishes to invite me out.

It is very easy to be
gratuitous with the people's money; it is easy to spend it in this way, but the people must work hard for it.
Is there any relation between the size of the motor cars and the size of the ministers concerned?
No, I think they depend more on the size of the ministers' hearts.
Does the size of the car have anything to do with the efficiency of the minister?
I think so.

Do any of the deputy
ministers use government cars free?
Yes, I think so.
How many?

I think they all do, but
if my hon. friend will refer to a return laid on the table a short time ago he will find all the details.

Here is an item which
illustrates the principle which I was asking the minister to elucidate. We have the details of expenditures for fittings in various branches of the public service; why should we vote this amount of $175,000 without details and with no knowledge of what is covered by it? We voted an amount for a pick-up table for Saskatoon, another for Cal-

Private Bills
gary and another for Regina, but now we are asked to vote $175,000 with no details at all-

Before the minister answers that question I might point out another similar ease. In this same item we have an amount of $420,000 for heating, salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen, and the item following the one now under consideration provides another $405,000 for heating. What is the reason for that?

One item is for Ottawa and the other is for outside places. With regard to the question of the leader of the opposition I might say that we must supply these fittings to the various offices during the year, and we can only judge the details by what we supplied last year.
That is exactly the point. What does this amount cover? Is it for filing cabinets and that sort of thing?

Furniture and fittings for
offices generally.

Should not the requisitions be available before the estimates are submitted, in order that the government might know exactly what is required? That has been done in connection with the other items I have mentioned.
A great many of these requisitions come in from month to month.
Are there any new buildings to fit out? What is the reason for the increase? There is a very substantial increase over last year's estimate, and that was an increase over previous years.

I might answer that question by stating that the chief architect's memorandum, which was submitted some time before the estimates were prepared, suggested a vote of $200,000 for this year. We must rely very largely upon the requisitions of the chief architect, who has had a great deal of experience in connection with these matters. He recommended that the appropriation for 1929-30 be increased to $200,000, but we decided that we would try to keep it down to a minimum of $175,000. The vote for furniture and fittings for buildings was $135,000 for 1928-29.

And what amount was
spent?

We spent $134,909. According to the memorandum submitted by the chief architect, as far back as June 30 the vote was over-engaged by $3,662, to meet the demands. Since that date the over-engagement has been steadily going up until on the 14th instant the very best we were
able to do was something around $19,000. In addition to this over-engagement the chief architect says he is holding requisitions which are estimated to cost approximately 823,000 to fill, and there are further orders which have been placed on condition that the parties wait for payment until the next fiscal year, which amount to approximately $4,000. There are accounts outstanding amounting to $3,700.
I would point out to the minister that this item was only $125,000 in 1926-27 and $125,000 in 1925-26; the further this government goes along the more extravagant it seems to get.

the consideration of these bills have objected only to the procedure which we follow, and which is not thorough. We cannot deal satisfactorily with these cases in this way. The amendment moved to-night is at least evidence of a desire on the part of some hon. members to provide some protection for the women and children involved in divorce suits. At the same time, although I do not agree that this house and the senate should be devoting their time to the consideration of divorce cases, instead of passing a bill to establish a divorce court in Ontario, from which province most of the divorces come, I am of the opinion that now that we have served notice on the house and to the country at large that the present procedure is unsatisfactory, we can do nothing better this session than grant the divorces that have come 'before us, disposing of the cases in the best manner we can. In my view that would be the best course to follow. On a previous occasion I objected to this procedure because I felt that there should be an expression of opinion on the part of the house that in its judgment, after several years' experience, the present practice had proved unsatisfactory. In many provinces, including the province in which I live, there are divorce courts, and I can say to every hon. member that divorces are very much better disposed of in those courts than they are by the method which we are obliged to follow in this house. I cannot see that we are going to gain very much by simply blocking the passage of these bills, although I do not suggest for a moment that anyone is blocking intentionally. As I see it, the motive is to bring more forcibly to the attention of the house and of the country the undesirable character of the present procedure which we are obliged to follow in passing divorce bills. There are some hon. members who are strongly opposed to the principle of divorce, but I do not think the principle is at all at stake in the discussion of these bills.

In this case the petitioner and respondent were married in the year 1911 and subsequently lived in Fort William, Ontario, until 1921, when the respondent left home. In 1925 she was found living in Vancouver under the name of Mrs. Edgar D. Casseday. Evidence was given before the divorce committee of the senate by an independent witness, a former resident of Fort William, who happened to be residing at Vancouver, as to the circumstances under which the respondent was living there. She had apparently obtained a divorce in Minnesota and had married this man, and they were living together as man and wife.

I must thank the
hon. member for such a clear statement; it is one of the best we have had. I am satisfied except on one point. I understand this woman obtained a divorce in the United States. Are not United States divorces recognized in such cases?
No.
I should like to have the legal point explained.

American divorces are not recognized in this country. The petitioner and respondent were domiciled in Fort William at the time the wife left home. Apparently she went to Minnesota and there acquired domicile which enabled her to obtain a divorce according to the laws of that state. But that divorce is not recognized in Canada, and, so far as our laws are concerned, she has in fact committed bigamy in remarrying.

A judgment to that effect was rendered in Montreal in the past month, in which it was held by Judge Lacroix that Canadians securing divorces in the United States remained, in the eyes of Canadian law, married to the first partner.

We ought to have some statement of the case from the Minister of Justice. There are literally thousands of Canadians who have obtained divorces in the United States. In the phrase used in these bills, are they all to-day, "living in adultery"? Is the second marriage unrecognized and are their children by such marriage illegitimate? There are far-reaching consequences involved in the question.

The minister has doubtless seen in his own department the plans which were prepared many years ago looking to the construction of a very fine series of buildings on the far side of Wellington street from the Rideau club down to the Bank of Montreal corner. I am not quite certain who prepared those plans, but my memory is that it was a very distinguished architect, and the late Mr. Ewart used to exhibit them with some degree of pride. After they had carefully considered the situation it was found that that site on Wellington street from the Rideau club to

the Victoria chambers would cost a great deal of money, because banks, the club building and other buildings were in occupation, and the space would be somewhat less than what was available on the land west of the supreme court building. Those buildings were acquired partly by agreement and partly by expropriation, if my memory serves me aright. For the moment I am speaking only from memory. It gave the government a great deal of concern as to whether they should endeavour to take the property in front of the parliament buildings or the property west of the supreme court building. But if I remember correctly, in view of the fact that there was nearly twice as much property west of the supreme court building as there was from the Rideau club to the Victoria chambers, it was thought desirable to acquire the former property having regard to future requirements and the fact that you could not carry the Wellington street property out to Sparks street without expending too much money, whereas the property west of the supreme court building was between the river and the street. Accordingly that land was acquired, extending west of the supreme court building a considerable distance-I do not know how many feet it is- and a complete scheme worked out for a series of buildings. I presume the Confederation block, so-called, is the first unit in that building scheme.

I think I have in mind the scheme to which my hon. friend refers. After several contests by different planners and architects, the scheme of which the Confederation building is the beginning was finally decided upon, but it is not exactly the same as that referred to by my hon. friend.

No, but the general terms are much the same. It will be recalled that a commission was appointed headed by Sir Herbert Holt to make a report upon the city improvement generally. It will be recalled what the government did. This is the point of the criticism. The government undertook improvements and the beautification of Ottawa, and to carry out those improvements and that beautification spent something like $3,000,000 acquiring the property comprising the square near the post office, the Russell hotel building, and other buildings in that locality. But if the object is to beautify and improve, the government did just the exact opposite of what it had in mind when it let the structure on the corner opposite the Bank of Montreal, on the site of the old Victoria chambers building, be erected. When this vast scheme of building west of the supreme court buildings 
was undertaken, the government then had in mind the provision of office accommodation for all the public service in Ottawa, looking forward for half a century. That was the general conception of the undertaking. Then when the town planning commission made their report-it will be remembered that an engineer came from Chicago to Ottawa-the commission at the head of which was Sir Herbert Holt made certain recommendations, and in a broad and general way this park that you now have in front of the post office follows the report of the commission, though not in detail. The difficulty-I confess I have never been able to solve it-is how you can talk of the beautification and improvement of Ottawa when in front of this magnificent ten million dollar structure you permit that building to be placed on the comer. The minister says that it could not be prevented, but the hon. member for South Toronto has made it perfectly clear that there was an opportunity, and that opportunity should have been grasped instead of spending three million dollars on the acquisition of the properties to which I have referred.
May I say this further? I think it is abundantly clear that the property between the Rideau Club and the Victoria chambers would not be sufficient to give effect to the plans that were in mind at that time for the accommodation of the public service of this country, and the location of the build'-ings on the site west of the supreme court buildings became a necessity because there was no other site to which you could easily go, unless you did as was done in Australia, move the capital entirely away from the city.
While on the subject of the Confederation building, and to obviate the necessity of speaking again, may I say, although the matter is perhaps not strictly relevant to the item under discussion, that something should be done with respect to the building in which the Supreme Court of Canada is housed. The Minister of Public Works is a member of the legal profession, and is no doubt aware that there are very valuable books in that library that cannot be replaced with money. The building was an old carpenter shop in 1878, and it is now the home of the highest court in Canada. I cannot but think that, finding money as we have done for many other purposes, we should not permit this condition to continue. The present structure is finished inside with highly inflammable wood-white pine-much of it hand-carved and covered with shellac which will burn practically if you put a match against it. The greatest possible care must be exer-

Supply-Public Works-Victoria
cised on the part of everybody about the premises to prevent the building being burned down. Such a loss-I am speaking merely as a member of the legal profession-would be very hard to contemplate; for there are books there that cannot be replaced. It is also very unpleasant to reflect on the fact that the home of the highest court in Canada, what we speak of as being the court of last resort in this country, should be housed in an old carpenter shop, to which some improvements, very few, have been made since 1878. If I were asked to-day to say what public service in Ottawa I regard as being most in need of a new public building, I would say that it is the Supreme Court of Canada. That is my profound conviction. I have been over most of that building. It is neither fire proof nor commodious. The minister this afternoon said that it took eight charwomen and one foreman daily to look after it, just keeping it in shape. Look at the floors and everything connected with it! If governments are trustees alike for this generation and the next, I would say that no greater trusteeship rests upon them than that of providing decent facilities for the Supreme Court of Canada. I was surprised to find in the estimates no appropriation for this purpose. I would strongly impress upon the minister and through him upon the administration, the necessity of taking action in this matter. After all, in the ultimate analysis law and the maintenance of the rule and reign of law is what all governments must have in mind, and if you do not house 'in decent premises, an institution such as the Supreme Court of Canada, you are going to have an unfavourable reaction in the matter of the general conduct of litigation and the maintenance of law and order in this country.

Has the minister taken into consideration the desirability of improving the acoustic properties of the chamber? Many times we do not know what is going on, especially when exchanges are taking place between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition. We do not want to sit here and be dummies, we want to know what-

Supply-Public Works-Ottawa
is going on. It is rather annoying to any hon. member who has the floor to be told to speak louder, and it is still more annoying to us to have to cry " louder."

If we all had as good voices as some of my hon. friends opposite there would not be as much difficulty about the acoustics of this chamber. And if those members who talk almost continuously when discussion is going on would desist it would obviate a lot of our difficulty. The matter has received a good deal of attention. In 1922 a report was submitted regarding the acoustics of the chamber by Professor F. A. Saunders, of Harvard university, Cambridge, Massachusetts.
I thought it was Cambridge, England.

Before reading his memorandum I might observe, having been in another legislative chamber for some time, that this difficulty occurs periodically in every such chamber in the country. I know of none where complaints of this kind are not made, arising from the fact that the speakers are not arranged as they are in the ordinary auditorium. The arrangement in any of these legislative chambers is particularly difficult, but it has never been considered advisable to adopt the auditorium style. The statements which I shall read to the committee were made by the man who is considered the highest authority on the subject. He submitted his report in 1922 and again on June 26, 1926. He suggested that heavy curtains be hung in front of gallery openings and the openings under the side galleries, and that a heavy carpet be placed on the floor. This was done. Heavy insulating paper was also put under the carpet. The suggestions Professor Saunders made at that time were carried out. Complaints again arose regarding the acoustics, and Professor Saunders further reported after examination that he did not see how the acoustics could be further improved. Writing to the architect, he states:
As I have just returned from a visit to the houses of parliament at your suggestion^ to consider the acoustical properties of the Commons chamber especially, I desire to send in a report of my investigation.
Four years ago you asked me to look over these same chambers, and I found at that time that they were not quite satisfactory. The acoustical treatment which had been recommended for them eight years ago by Mr. C. M. Swan, of New York, to Mr. Pearson had not been completely carried out. . . .
My conclusion is that both of these chambers are now entirely satisfactory and I strongly recommend that no further changes be made.
The acoustical requirements of such a chamber are particularly exacting. The room must be large, and the speakers placed in all possible positions with respect to the hearers; yet it is expected that a man speaking often only in a conversational tone will be audible from any point on the floor, or perhaps in the whole chamber.
It is a well known fact that sound produced in a room reaches the ear of a hearer by many paths. The direct line from the speaker is the ceiling, etc, and if these surfaces are hard, and reflect a large proportion of the sound energy falling upon them, the listener hears a much louder sound than otherwise. It is obvious, however, that this loudness is due to sound arriving late	
He goes on with a scientific dissertation on sound which is not very intelligible to me. Then he continues:
In my opinion this process has been carried out to just the right extent in both chambers. . . .
As a result of the tests, I feel sure that the house chamber is unusual in the clarity with which speech of very moderate volume can be heard and understood in it. When the house is not in session, an ordinary conversational tone is loud enough to be audible if one listens, and if one is not disturbed by extraneous sounds.
I submit that the greatest disturbance in this chamber comes from those who are talking while someone is trying to make himself heard, and no arrangement anyone can make will overcome that difficulty.
Perhaps it might be overcome if those in control would keep better order.

Yes, and we are all in
control more or less.
Mostly less.

He continues:
It would hardly be wise, however, to count on so small a volume of sound being satisfactory when the house is in session. Yet, it was obvious when 1 was there that many of the members do not raise their voices materially above the ordinary conversational level in addressing the house. It may 'be an effect of the extraordinarily good acoustical qualities of the room that the members may sometimes think a low tone is sufficient, but when the press representatives and the public in the gallery are to hear, it seems to be absolutely necessary that the speakers should use as loud a tone as they would in any other hall, addressing an equal number of persons.
At your suggestion, I have also considered the question of supplying the house chamber with microphones and loud speakers. On the whole, my recommendation is decidedly adverse.
The report is quite lengthy and he refers later on to the curtain arrangements. The curtains of course should be kept as nearly as possible closed in order to facilitate hearing. And they are usually left partly open at any

What has been done in that respect?

That question was considered and it was decided that while it might be advantageous to install some such system we had not yet reached the time here when it was necessary to resort to a device of that kind. It was felt that it would 'be better for the member to depend upon the clock in front of him and the clock to his right and to endeavour to follow the time as nearly as he could. The	information	given
by the minister is about what I desired. I thoroughly agree with him in the advantages of a central heating plant; there can be no question of that, and the system we now have was quite up-to-date when it was installed. Now, however, the minister tells us that it is proposed to install two additional boilers of 500 horse-power each with mechanical stokers, and that is where I part company with him. Mechanical stokers firing boilers of that character in my judgment are a thing of the past. I would strongly urge upon him that he put in equipment which will use
pulverized fuel. I would point out the great advance which has been made in that direction in the old country within the last two years, and particularly within the last year, during which very large installations of that character have been made with the very best results. I do not need to go into my reasons for advocating this system, but I would urge the minister to take the matter into very serious consideration before committing himself to another installation such as we have to-day, good though it may be. Its day ha3 gone by; a much better and more economical system can be put in, and I think it should be considered.

If an entirely new system were being installed now I think my hon. friend's argument would be very good, but the serious objection to heating with pulverized fuel is that the whole plant we have at present would have to be changed.

I am not advocating the change of the existing plant; I am advocating the adoption of powdered fuel in the two new units which are to be installed. There is no reason why the two systems should conflict at all; it will not be necessary to disturb one single unit of the existing plant if you equip the new plant to burn powdered fuel.

Well, much as I value
my hon. friend's opinion in the matter, the advice of my engineers hardly corresponds with his suggestion. Then there is the objection with regard to the smoke or soot being greater if pulverized fuel is used.

We have a heating plant in the city of Winnipeg which uses pulverized fuel and we do not have any difficulty with regard to smoke.
